title: Hillel the Elder told a gentile, on one foot: "What is hateful to thee, do not unto thy fellow man", this is the whole Torah

trailer.text: Hillel the Elder was a Jewish sage and teacher, and according to My Jewish Learning he served as head of the Sanhedrin and founded the House of Hillel.

According to the Babylonian Talmud, a gentile asked to convert on condition that he be taught the entire Torah while standing on one foot, and Shammai pushed him away with the builder's cubit that was in his hand.
The man came to Hillel, and Hillel said to him: "What is hateful to thee, do not unto thy fellow man", that is, what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow, and this is the whole Torah.
"And the rest is its commentary", Hillel added, and now one must go and study, and he converted the man himself.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Hillel saw love of man as the kernel of the entire Jewish teaching.

paragraphs.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Hillel was a Babylonian by birth.
According to the Forward, he came to the Land of Israel at the age of 40 and devoted another 40 years to the study of Torah.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, it is misguided to try to derive precise historical information from these numbers.
According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, in Jerusalem Hillel studied under Shmaiah and Abtalion.
According to the entry on Hillel on the Encyclopedia.com website, in Jerusalem Hillel studied at the academy of Shmaiah and Abtalion and earned a meager living as a laborer.
According to one story cited by My Jewish Learning, he was so poor that he could not pay the admission fee to the study hall.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, it is narrated that the Bene Bathyra voluntarily resigned their position in favor of Hillel.
After that, Hillel was recognized as the highest authority among the Pharisees and the scribes of Jerusalem.
According to My Jewish Learning, Hillel served as head of the Sanhedrin, the ancient rabbinic tribunal.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the talmudic versions of the appointment story probably do not reflect ancient and reliable historical traditions.
According to the Talmud, a gentile came before Shammai.
He asked to convert on condition that he be taught the entire Torah while standing on one foot.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, he asked for a summary of the Jewish religion in the most concise terms.
According to the Forward, Shammai was offended by a request that seemed ludicrous to him and chased the man away.
According to the Talmud, Shammai pushed him away with the builder's cubit that was in his hand.
The New World Encyclopedia describes this as driving him away with a measuring rod.
The man went to Hillel.
Hillel said to him: "De'alakh sani lehavrakh la ta'aved".
What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; this is the entire Torah, and the rest is its commentary.
Then he added that one must go and study.
Hillel converted the man.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Hillel saw love of man as the kernel of the entire Jewish teaching.
The same source says that with these words Hillel recognized the Biblical precept of brotherly love, Leviticus chapter nineteen, verse 18, as the fundamental principle of the Jewish moral law.

stations.title: Four Hundred Zuz and Three Converts

paragraphs.text: The man came on a Friday, while Hillel was washing his head, and Hillel wrapped himself and went out to him.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, they questioned him and made insulting allusions to his Babylonian origin, but did not succeed in angering him.

According to My Jewish Learning, the man told Hillel that he had lost four hundred zuz because of him, and Hillel replied that he should be careful with his temper, for Hillel is worthy of having four hundred zuz and another four hundred zuz lost on his account, and Hillel will not be upset.
According to My Jewish Learning, three people came in turn to Shammai and then to Hillel, and asked to convert for insincere reasons.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the story presents them as rejected by Shammai and accepted by Hillel.
In time the three said that Shammai's impatience sought to drive them from the world, and Hillel's humility brought them near, under the wings of the Divine Presence.
According to My Jewish Learning, the sages taught that a person should always be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai.
According to Chabad.org, Hillel was a very humble and patient man, and there are many stories that illustrate this.

stations.title: Sayings, Enactments and the House of Hillel

paragraphs.text: According to the New World Encyclopedia, one of Hillel's famous sayings is: "If I am not for myself, then who will be for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?"
The same source cites his saying: do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place.
According to the Encyclopedia of Religion, in Pirkei Avot he calls on people to be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace.
The prosbul protected the creditor against the loss of his property, and the needy against being refused a loan for fear of loss.

According to My Jewish Learning, the Talmud records hundreds of disputes between Hillel and Shammai, with the House of Hillel generally tending toward leniency and the House of Shammai toward stringency.
According to My Jewish Learning, Hillel was known more for his kindness and ethics than for his legal rulings.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the Talmud relates that Hillel had 80 students.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, when he died they lamented him: "Wo for the meek one! Wo for the pious! Wo for the disciple of Ezra!"
He remained in the memory of posterity as a teacher who taught and practised the virtues of philanthropy, fear of God and humility.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, his descendants established a dynasty that dominated rabbinic circles in the Land of Israel for more than 400 years.
According to My Jewish Learning, at every Passover seder Hillel is mentioned at "korech", the joining together of matzah, bitter herbs and haroset, in memory of his custom.
The Jewish student organization Hillel International has borne his name since its founding in 1923.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the name was chosen by Rabbi Benjamin Frankel, the first director of Jewish campus activity at the University of Illinois.
According to the website Israel in Their Land, the Knesset Menorah in Jerusalem portrays Hillel teaching a man Torah while standing on one foot.
According to My Jewish Learning, his grave is in Meron, in northern Israel.

stations.title: What Cannot Be Known for Certain

paragraphs.text: According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, even the earliest rabbinic sources on Hillel are highly legendary.
According to the Forward, very little is known about the historical Hillel.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, a later tradition assigned him to the family of David.
According to the Encyclopedia of Religion, most scholars do not take this seriously, because Davidic ancestry was also claimed for others.
According to the Encyclopedia of Religion, the negative formulation of the rule, which later developed into the "Golden Rule", has parallels in ancient literature, such as the Book of Tobit.

According to the New World Encyclopedia, many scholars have noticed similarities between Hillel's sayings and the teachings of Jesus, and some have speculated that Jesus was influenced by him or by his school.
According to the Forward, Rabbi Joseph Telushkin wrote a book about Hillel from an implicitly Orthodox perspective, and the non-Orthodox may bristle at some of his assumptions.

versions.says: According to My Jewish Learning, he is said to have been born in Babylonia around 110 BCE and to have died in Jerusalem in the first years of the Common Era, although this has not been clearly established
According to the Forward, he lived from around 110 BCE to 10 CE
According to the Encyclopedia of Religion, he lived from around 50 BCE to the beginning of the first century CE
According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, lived from about 60 BCE to approximately 10 CE
According to the website Israel in Their Land, he died in 8 CE
According to the New World Encyclopedia, he lived around the beginning of the Common Era and died in 10–20 CE

quote_translations.c2: Convert me on condition that you teach me the entire Torah while I am standing on one foot. He pushed him away with the builder's cubit that was in his hand. He came before Hillel; he converted him.
quote_translations.c1: He said to him: That which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow – this is the entire Torah, and the rest – it is its commentary; go and study.
quote_translations.c15: Hillel (הלל) was a famous Jewish religious teacher who lived in Jerusalem during the time of King Herod around the beginning of the Common Era (d. 10-20 C.E.).
quote_translations.c202611284: One of them said: I will provoke him. That day was Shabbat eve, and Hillel was washing his head.
quote_translations.c202611285: He wrapped himself and went out to greet him.
quote_translations.c202611288: Some time later, the three of them gathered in one place. They said: Shammai's impatience sought to drive us from the world.
quote_translations.c202611289: Hillel's humility brought us under the wings of the Divine Presence.
